A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RvLLM framework and three case studies, with readable text, equations, figures, and tables. v1 ends after its references despite mentioning appendices; v3 includes Appendices A–G. The supplied documents support a reliable comparison of their reported content.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on railway-law violation detection, numerical comparison, and inequality solving, including detection rates, error counts, and execution times in Tables 1–3.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds evaluations against other verification methods, including detection rates and token usage in Appendix E.

M1.justification: The ESL-based procedure retains Level-1/Level-2 interpretation, rule normalization, forward chaining, and follow-up query generation. v1 Sections 3–4 correspond to v3 Sections 2–3. Added prompts and worked examples document the existing procedure without establishing an algorithmic change.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same three task domains using 304 railway-law scenarios, 100 generated numerical comparisons, and 40 A-Level inequality problems. Appendix B supplies dataset descriptions, and Appendix D illustrates an existing task; neither establishes additional dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds evaluated SelfCheckGPT and domain-constraint prompt augmentation, termed LLM-as-a-judge, across all three tasks (Figure 3 and Tables 3, 9–11). v1 discusses SelfCheckGPT in related work but provides no corresponding experimental comparison. These additions substantially broaden the comparator set.

E3.justification: New comparisons introduce selected target-model subsets and a stated common DeepSeek-V3 verifier/judge configuration in Appendix E, although this is not reconciled with the main text's same-model setting. Inequality evaluation expands beyond erroneous answers to report TNR on correct answers and token costs. Legal class counts change from 280 unsafe/24 safe to 281/23; this does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds a detailed error case tracing how RvLLM identifies an animal-transport violation missed by Qwen-plus. Appendix E adds a token-cost comparison for inequality verification. Existing inequality error-category and perception-agent analyses are retained, without new robustness or sensitivity sweeps.

E5.justification: Unlike v1, Appendix F reports preliminary runs until outputs stabilize and asserts negligible variance at temperature 0.5. This adds qualitative repeatability information, but supplies no run counts, seeds, measured dispersion, confidence intervals, or significance tests. It does not establish increased replication.

E6.justification: Figure 3 and Tables 3, 9–11 add cross-method detection results and inequality token costs. Existing results also change: Qwen 2.5 (7B) inequality errors increase from 23 to 25, with DeepSeek-based detection changing from 52.2% to 48% (v1 Table 3; v3 Table 4). Legal Qwen-turbo combined TPR changes from 75% to 74.7%. Numerical-comparison Table 2 is unchanged; the revisions do not demonstrate same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: The core definitions and transformation equations remain unchanged, but Appendix A adds a multi-step mathematical forward-chaining derivation on another rule set. This example is internally inconsistent: its final inference uses ¬M∧K⇒N, absent from the initially stated rules. No new general theorem or proof is supplied.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains ESL and domain-informed runtime verification. v3 adds an introduction and conclusion claim that RvLLM achieves a better TPR/TNR balance than existing runtime detection methods, extending v1's effectiveness claims to explicit comparative superiority.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly conditions soundness on faithful expert encoding and describes specification/perception errors and bias as limitations (Section 3 and Appendix G). Appendix E attributes comparative performance to separating language understanding from symbolic reasoning. It removes v1's conjecture that DeepSeek-V3 favors language understanding over logical reasoning and the conclusion's explicit single-reasoning-strategy limitation.

D1.justification: v3 supplies the prompt documentation absent from the supplied v1: original queries, perception prompts, Level-2 instantiation, and follow-up templates in Appendix C. Appendices B, D–F add generation constraints, dataset examples, a worked specification, baseline configurations, and temperature information. These substantially improve implementation transparency without proving changes to the original implementation.

R1.justification: v3 adds an 'Expert systems with NLP' discussion connecting RvLLM to earlier symbolic/NLP systems, including SHRDLU and MedLEE. It also adds references on unit propagation and propagation completeness. Existing LLM-testing and runtime-verification positioning remains largely intact, making this a focused extension.

P1.justification: Related work moves from Section 2 to Section 5, and Appendices A–D substantially expand the exposition through forward-chaining, dataset, prompting, and application walkthroughs. Additional comparison, statistical, and broader-impact discussions reorganize the explanatory structure, although much of the original method prose remains intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds comparative bar charts, a four-panel forward-chaining illustration, nine prompt figures, and several case-study and comparison tables. Existing figures are resized/repositioned, and Table 2 moves beside the new comparison table. Appendix Tables 9–10 partly redisplay or extend main-text comparisons rather than representing wholly separate experiments.

improvement.justification: v1 lacks evaluated runtime-method competitors and the prompt appendices it references. v3 substantially addresses both deficiencies through actual baseline comparisons, inequality false-positive and cost results, and detailed dataset/prompt documentation. These materially improve assessability and reproducibility. The gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: inconsistent verifier-model descriptions, unsupported negligible-variance assertions in Appendix F, and the flawed worked derivation in Appendix A.
